blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — individualized bed-rail risk assessment, entrapment, and climbing-related falls in confused older adults
stem: A confused older adult repeatedly tries to climb over full-length bed rails. Which safety concern should the nurse recognize?

options.A: Continue the full-length rails and increase rounding, because the observed climbing reflects confusion rather than a safety problem created by the rails.
options.B: Lower the bed and add floor mats while leaving the full-length rails unchanged, because alternative fall measures remove the need to reassess rail-related risk.
options.C: Pad the rail openings and keep all rails raised, because padding addresses entrapment and makes climbing over the rails an acceptable residual risk.
options.D: Reassess whether the rails are increasing risk; confused older adults may become entrapped or sustain more serious falls when they climb over bed rails.

rationale: D is correct. Current FDA hospital-bed safety resources identify frail, elderly, and confused patients as especially vulnerable to bed-rail entrapment and state that climbing over bed rails can result in more serious fall injuries. FDA also recommends individual patient assessment before routine bed-rail use and advises that rail selection/placement should discourage climbing. Therefore, repeated attempts to climb over full-length rails should trigger reassessment of whether the rails are increasing rather than reducing this client's risk. A is incorrect because observed climbing is itself a rail-related safety concern. B is incomplete because adding other fall-reduction measures does not remove the need to reassess a rail that may be contributing to harm. C is incorrect because padding may address some openings but does not eliminate the climbing-related fall hazard or replace individualized assessment.
educational_objective: Reassess bed-rail use in confused older adults because rails can create entrapment and climbing-related fall hazards rather than reliably preventing injury.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Hospital Beds; A Guide to Bed Safety — Bed Rails in Hospitals, Nursing Homes and Home Health Care; Recommendations for Health Care Providers Using Adult Portable Bed Rails; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current FDA hospital-bed and bed-rail safety resources rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: FDA Hospital Beds current page lines 57-66: most entrapment reports involved frail, elderly or confused patients and healthcare facilities should use Clinical Guidance to assess individual patient needs before side-rail use. FDA A Guide to Bed Safety, Patient Safety section: bed-rail risks include entrapment and more serious injuries from falls when patients climb over rails; patients with memory or unsafe ambulation problems require careful assessment. FDA Recommendations for Health Care Providers Using Adult Portable Bed Rails: avoid routine bed-rail use without individual assessment and select/place rails to discourage climbing that could lead to falls. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control detailed content covers injury prevention, restraint/safety-device use, and safe equipment use.
source_claim_supported: Fresh current FDA evidence directly supports increased entrapment vulnerability in elderly/confused patients, more serious injuries from climbing over bed rails, and individualized assessment rather than routine rail use. The item does not claim that rails are never appropriate; it tests reassessment when the observed behavior suggests the rail may be increasing risk.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — accident/error/injury prevention, safe use of equipment, and use/reassessment of restraints or safety devices, detailed content pp. 24-26.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — relevant official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control pages were freshly screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation. FDA evidence used for Q0315 is current HTML; no FDA PDF evidence is relied on for the final key.
correction_summary: Original Q0315 had a uniquely longest correct answer and an absolute-word distractor. The item was rebuilt with four balanced, plausible nursing interpretations. The key now tests the clinically important FDA principle that a confused older adult climbing over full-length rails may face increased entrapment and fall injury risk and therefore requires individualized reassessment rather than routine continuation of the rails.

option_audit.A: Plausible monitoring-focused response; incorrect because the observed climbing is itself evidence that the rails may be creating risk.
option_audit.B: Plausible multimodal fall-prevention response; incorrect because adding alternatives does not eliminate the need to reassess a potentially hazardous rail setup.
option_audit.C: Plausible entrapment-mitigation response; incorrect because padding does not resolve climbing-related fall risk or replace individualized assessment.
option_audit.D: Correct; directly reflects FDA evidence on entrapment, climbing-related falls, and individualized assessment.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on simplistic all/only/always/never wording as the reason it is wrong.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 153, B 160, C 148, D 152 characters; the key is not longest and there is no positive length cue.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are realistic safety-management interpretations and differ in whether the observed rail-related risk is reassessed rather than in obvious wording quality.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified in the pre-stage audit. A ignores the rail-related hazard, B leaves the rail risk unresolved, and C addresses openings without resolving climbing-related injury risk. Post-fetch adversarial reread remains required.
